# Algorithmic Persuasion, Cognitive Depletion, and Online Impulse Buying: A Systematic Review and Dynamic Dual-Path S-O-R Framework (2018-2026) **Author:** Le Phuc Hai (Lê Phúc Hải) **Affiliation:** NCSKIT.org (Independent Research Group) **ORCID:** [https://orcid.org/0009-0004-1215-5023](https://orcid.org/0009-0004-1215-5023) **Correspondence:** [hailp@ncskit.org](mailto:hailp@ncskit.org) --- ## HIGHLIGHTS - Synthesizes 866 studies on AI recommenders and impulse buying (2018-2026). - Uncovers four clusters via VOSviewer, with Dark Side newest (APY = 2024.4). - Separates cold-start fluency from cumulative e-satisfaction (P4a-P4b). - Contrasts competing cognitive-affective interactions (b3 > 0 vs. b3 < 0). - Links tiered ethical friction to EU DSA/FTC principles and A/B trials. --- ## ABSTRACT The rapid deployment of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered personalized recommendation systems across digital retailing platforms has substantially altered consumer browsing dynamics, shifting electronic commerce from deliberate keyword-driven search toward algorithmically curated discovery. While practitioners deploy predictive and generative algorithms to stimulate conversion, academic inquiry into the cognitive-affective mechanics governing AI-mediated impulsive consumption remains theoretically fragmented. Following PRISMA 2020 reporting principles and the TCCM framework, this study conducts a systematic literature review and bibliometric science mapping on 2,458 initial records retrieved from the Dimensions scholarly database (January 2018 to November 2026), retaining peer-reviewed journal articles with valid DOIs after excluding preprints, books, monographs, and grants. After deduplication (1,441 unique records) and two-stage eligibility screening, 866 focal studies were mapped in VOSviewer. Bibliometric mapping reveals four thematic clusters: (1) Algorithmic Recommendation Stimuli (Cluster 1 - Red); (2) Cognitive Organism and E-Satisfaction (Cluster 2 - Green); (3) Affective Organism and Impulsive Behavioral Response (Cluster 3 - Blue); and (4) The Dark Side of Personalization: Algorithmic Surveillance, Privacy Reactance, and Self-Control Fatigue (Cluster 4 - Yellow), which emerges as the most recent research frontier (mean $\text{APY} = 2024.4$). Advancing beyond static additive S-O-R models, we formulate a Dynamic Dual-Path S-O-R Framework contrasting Generation 1.0 collaborative filtering with Generation 2.0 conversational Generative AI. We separate in-session cognitive fluency (cold-start) from cumulative e-satisfaction (repeat sessions) and specify competing interaction hypotheses ($b_3 > 0$ synergistic permission vs. $b_3 < 0$ hot/cool override). We further integrate endogenous surveillance reactance (P1), candidate self-regulatory strain (P7a/P7b), and a recursive post-purchase regret loop (P8), concluding with a 5-pillar research agenda and regulatory-aligned A/B testing propositions. **Keywords**: Artificial Intelligence; Personalized Recommendation Systems; Online Impulse Buying; Dual-Path S-O-R Model; PRISMA 2020; VOSviewer Bibliometrics; Cognitive Fit Theory; Ego Depletion; Algorithmic Dark Patterns. --- ## 1. INTRODUCTION ### 1.1. Background and The Algorithmic Retailing Paradigm Shift In contemporary digital retailing ecosystems, consumers no longer navigate static, hierarchical category trees (Shanahan et al., 2019; Xiao & Benbasat, 2018). Instead, they are continuously enveloped within dynamic, hyper-personalized information streams driven by deep neural collaborative filtering, transformer-based sequential recommenders, and real-time behavioral telemetry (Al-Natour et al., 2011; Hallikainen et al., 2022). The foundational architecture of consumer discovery has shifted from deliberative, keyword-driven item retrieval (*search-based shopping*) to serendipitous, algorithmically triggered consumption (*discovery-based shopping*) (Sundar & Kim, 2019; Wang et al., 2022). Building on foundational digital retailing frameworks (Dwivedi et al., 2021; Guha et al., 2021), the proliferation of Large Language Model (LLM)-powered conversational shopping agents and Generative AI interfaces between 2023 and 2026 (Do Xuan Nguyen & Nguyen, 2026; Huang & Ahmad, 2026; Pang et al., 2026) enables platforms to anticipate and shape latent consumer desires in real time. A primary behavioral outcome of this algorithmic immersion is online impulse buying (OIB) (defined as sudden, hedonically complex, and unplanned purchase decisions characterized by diminished deliberative cognitive evaluation) (Beatty & Ferrell, 1998; Rook & Fisher, 1995). Prior systematic reviews establish that unplanned purchasing constitutes a substantial share of digital commerce activity, catalyzed by algorithmic discovery feeds, flash recommendations, and frictionless one-click checkout infrastructures (Chan et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2019). While practitioners celebrate predictive personalization as an engine of customer lifetime value and transaction velocity, consumer psychologists express growing scholarly concern regarding the ethical boundaries of algorithmic nudging, choice architecture manipulation, and the erosion of consumer self-regulatory willpower (Baumeister, 2002; Kumaran & Shobhana, 2026; Sweller, 1988). ### 1.2. Problem Statement, Salience Audit, and Positioning Relative to Prior Reviews Despite substantial growth in empirical scholarship over the past decade, literature examining the nexus of AI recommendation systems and impulsive buying remains siloed across computer science, information systems (IS), and consumer psychology. A preliminary lexical salience scan of Title and Abstract fields across our 866-study corpus indicates that while 12.01% ($n = 104$) of abstracts explicitly invoke S-O-R framing, explicit Title/Abstract mentions of interaction or moderated-mediation terms (2.19%, $n = 19$), curvilinear or threshold terms (1.50%, $n = 13$), surveillance, reactance, or privacy-paradox terms (1.27%, $n = 11$), regret, dissonance, or product-return terms (3.58%, $n = 31$), and ego-depletion or decision-fatigue terms (0.69%, $n = 6$) remain sparse. As detailed in Section 2.3 and Appendix A, these Title/Abstract counts represent conservative lower bounds of lexical salience relative to full-corpus author/index keyword occurrences. Three core theoretical fault lines motivate our synthesis: 1. Theoretical Fragmentation of Algorithmic Stimuli (The S-O-R Disconnect): While the classical Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) paradigm (Mehrabian & Russell, 1974; Jacoby, 2002) provides an established environmental psychology foundation, early retail studies operationalized "Stimuli" primarily as static website atmospherics (e.g., color, layout, navigation structure; Eroglu et al., 2001). In algorithmic commerce, stimuli are dynamic, adaptive, and agentic. Crucially, literature exhibits sharp disagreement on whether algorithmic attributes, specifically *Perceived Personalization (PP)*, *Perceived Recommendation Accuracy (ACC)*, and *Recommendation Novelty & Serendipity (NOV)*, operate harmoniously or create conflicting psychological appraisals (Al-Natour et al., 2011; Ampadu et al., 2022; Gallin & Portes, 2024; Shanahan et al., 2019). 2. The Dual-Path Cognitive-Affective Divide (The Organismic Black Box): Existing literature often treats internal consumer organismic states as a monolithic construct. While some scholars emphasize cognitive evaluations like cumulative e-satisfaction (ESAT) (Oliver, 1980, 1993; Spreng et al., 1996), others argue that impulse buying is primarily an affective, visceral response driven by emotional arousal and hedonic flow (Beatty & Ferrell, 1998; Verhagen & van Dolen, 2011). Extant research has yet to fully reconcile how cumulative satisfaction interacts with immediate cold-start fluency and visceral urges, or when over-personalization induces perceived algorithmic surveillance and reactance (Komiak & Benbasat, 2006; Xiao & Benbasat, 2007, 2018). 3. The Intention-Behavior Gap and Self-Regulatory Boundaries: Traditional marketing models frequently conflate the psychological *urge to buy impulsively (UBI)* with the enacted *online impulse buying behavior (OIB)*. However, empirical consumer psychology demonstrates that an impulse urge does not inevitably result in transactional checkout (Badgaiyan & Verma, 2015; Rook & Fisher, 1995). Candidate self-regulatory mechanisms, including resource depletion (Baumeister, 2002; Baumeister et al., 2007; Vohs & Faber, 2007) alongside cognitive load theory (Sweller, 1988) and multilab replication debates (Hagger et al., 2016), require careful integration into dynamic models of algorithmic retailing. To clarify incremental positioning, Table 1 contrasts this review against prior landmark reviews and temporal S-O-R models (Chan et al., 2017; Mariani et al., 2022; Tobon & Abril, 2024; Kumaran & Shobhana, 2026). **Table 1: Positioning Against Prior Landmark Reviews and Temporal S-O-R Models** | Study | Scope & Corpus | Curvilinear Privacy / Reactance | Fluency vs. Cumulative ESAT | Competing Interaction ($b_3$) | Recursive Regret Loop | | :--- | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | | **Chan et al. (2017)** | Pre-AI online impulse buying SLR | No | No | No | No | | **Mariani et al. (2022)** | Broad AI in marketing & psychology SLR | Partial (Ethics) | No | No | No | | **Tobon & Abril (2024)** | Apparel e-tailer impulse & returns | No | No | No | Yes (Returns) | | **Kumaran & Shobhana (2026)** | GenAI synthetic urgency & regret | Yes (Urgency) | No | No | Partial | | **Current Study (2026)** | 866-study AI-impulse SLR + Dual-Path Agenda | Yes (Endogenous P1) | Yes (P4a vs. P4b) | Yes ($b_3 > 0$ vs. $b_3 < 0$) | Yes (P8 + ESM) | ### 1.3. Research Objectives and Formal Research Questions To resolve these theoretical fault lines, this study executes an integrative multi-method investigation combining the PRISMA 2020 systematic review protocol with VOSviewer science mapping and the TCCM synthesis framework. Specifically, we address three overarching research questions: - **RQ1**: *What is the intellectual structure, thematic cluster architecture, and temporal evolution of international scholarship investigating AI recommendation systems and online impulse buying?* - **RQ2**: *Through what dual-path cognitive-affective mechanisms do algorithmic stimuli influence consumer organismic states, and how do these states mediate the translation into impulsive purchasing urges and behaviors?* - **RQ3**: *What psychological and technological boundary conditions govern this translation, and what future research agenda and ethical guardrails are necessary for sustainable algorithmic retailing?* ### 1.4. Paper Structure The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 delineates the systematic review methodology, detailing the PRISMA 2020 protocol, search strings, TCCM framing, text-mining gap audit protocol, and VOSviewer co-occurrence parameters. Section 3 presents the bibliometric performance analysis, VOSviewer quantitative cluster metrics and science mapping, and the TCCM empirical synthesis matrix. Section 4 articulates the integrative conceptual framework, develops eight core theoretical propositions (P1-P8, encompassing cold-start vs. cumulative paths P4a/P4b, affective mediation P5a, competing interaction P5b, and regulatory strain P7a/P7b), and outlines an empirical testing strategy. Section 5 discusses theoretical contributions, tiered ethical friction implications, details the 5-pillar future research agenda, acknowledges study limitations, and concludes. ## 2. METHODOLOGY: THE PRISMA 2020 PROTOCOL AND BIBLIOMETRIC DESIGN ### 2.1. Methodological Design and Agnostic Search Strategy To prevent confirmation bias, the identification strategy adhered to an agnostic three-block Boolean structure covering technological stimuli (AI recommendation engines), behavioral outcomes (impulse purchasing), and digital retail contexts. Theoretical frameworks (such as S-O-R) and mediating constructs (such as e-satisfaction) were intentionally excluded from search strings so thematic clusters emerged inductively (Paul & Criado, 2020). Searches were executed on November 15, 2026 in the Dimensions scholarly database (`title_abstract` / full-data indexing), selected for its extensive coverage of interdisciplinary research across artificial intelligence, data science, and applied digital commerce. Large-scale bibliometric benchmarks by Thelwall (2018) and Visser et al. (2021) demonstrate that Dimensions achieves publication coverage comparable to, and in technology and applied computing domains often broader than, Scopus and Web of Science. Because Dimensions indexes diverse document types, rigorous programmatic filtering was applied to isolate peer-reviewed journal articles with valid Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs). The standardized conceptual Boolean query is shown below: ```text TITLE-ABS-KEY ( ( "artificial intelligence" OR "AI" OR "recommendation system*" OR "recommender system*" OR "algorithmic recommendation*" OR "personalized recommendation*" OR "deep learning recommendation*" OR "collaborative filtering" ) AND ( "impulse buying" OR "impulsive buying" OR "impulse purchase*" OR "spontaneous purchase*" OR "unplanned purchase*" OR "urge to buy impulsively" ) AND ( "e-commerce" OR "online shopping" OR "digital retailing" OR "electronic commerce" OR "social commerce" OR "mobile commerce" ) ) ``` ### 2.2. Eligibility Criteria and TCCM Framework Framing The screening protocol was framed around the TCCM Framework (Theory, Context, Characteristics, Methodology), recognized as a widely adopted framework for systematic reviews in marketing and retailing (Paul & Rosado-Serrano, 2019; Paul & Criado, 2020): - Theory (T): Studies examining behavioral, psychological, or information processing mechanisms (e.g., S-O-R, Cognitive Fit Theory, Dual-Process Theory, Self-Regulation). - Context (C): Digital retailing environments including electronic commerce, mobile retailing, social commerce, and livestream shopping platforms. - Characteristics (C): Algorithmic system attributes (personalization, accuracy, novelty, transparency) and consumer internal states (fluency, e-satisfaction, arousal, urge). - Methodology (M): Rigorous empirical investigations (laboratory experiments, field surveys, neuro-marketing, structural equation modeling, fsQCA) alongside foundational conceptual and systematic review benchmarks that establish core construct taxonomies. We established four explicit Inclusion Criteria (IC) and four Exclusion Criteria (EC): - **IC1**: Published in English in peer-reviewed scholarly journals between January 2018 and November 2026. - **IC2**: Empirical investigation or foundational conceptual/review benchmark explicitly analyzing AI/algorithmic recommendation features and consumer impulse buying dynamics. - **IC3**: For empirical studies, clear reporting of sample size, analytical technique, and theoretical grounding (foundational conceptual/review benchmarks retained under IC2 are exempted from sample-size reporting). - **IC4**: Indexed in Dimensions as a peer-reviewed journal article (`type = article`) carrying a valid, resolvable DOI. - **EC1**: Non-peer-reviewed and non-journal Dimensions records, including all Preprints, Monographs, Edited Books, Grants, editorials, commentaries, and conference abstracts. - **EC2**: Purely algorithmic optimization studies focusing solely on matrix factorization or loss function mathematics without measuring human behavioral responses. - **EC3**: Studies situated purely in brick-and-mortar physical stores with no digital recommendation interface. - **EC4**: Duplicate records across databases. ### 2.3. The 4-Stage Screening Funnel (2,458 to 866 Articles) Adhering to the PRISMA 2020 statement (Page et al., 2021), the data collection and screening process progressed through four transparent, auditable stages: 1. Identification: Database retrieval from Dimensions yielded 2,458 initial records after applying document-type restrictions (excluding grants, monographs, edited books, and preprints) to retain peer-reviewed journal candidates with valid DOIs. 2. Deduplication: Using R `bibliometrix` and a custom Python reconciliation script, 1,017 duplicate records were programmatically identified and removed using normalized DOI and title-Levenshtein distance matching, yielding 1,441 unique records entering the screening stage. 3. Screening (Title & Abstract): Two independent research assistants conducted blind title and abstract screening against IC1-IC4 and EC1-EC3, with the author serving as the senior third adjudicator. Inter-coder reliability was strong (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.89$; PABAK = 0.91). Disagreements on 34 articles at the Title/Abstract stage (and 18 marginal papers at the subsequent Full-Text stage) were adjudicated by the senior third reviewer, resulting in the exclusion of 496 irrelevant records (primarily technical benchmarking papers without human behavioral data), leaving 945 full-text articles. 4. Eligibility & Final Inclusion: All 945 full-text articles were evaluated in depth ($\kappa_{\text{FT}} = 0.87$), with 18 marginal cases resolved by the senior third reviewer (complementing the 34 Title/Abstract adjudications above). Of these, 79 articles were excluded due to incomplete empirical metrics ($n = 45$; e.g., missing sample sizes or reliability/validity indicators in empirical designs, while retaining foundational conceptual/review benchmarks under IC2) or lacking explicit impulse buying construct measures ($n = 34$). The final systematic synthesis and science mapping corpus comprises 866 peer-reviewed articles (within which a strict 3-pillar empirical core of $n = 167$ studies is flagged in the OSF screening ledger alongside the broader thematic corpus). All 866 studies were analyzed in VOSviewer using keyword co-occurrence network analysis ($T \ge 5$ occurrences, full counting with association strength normalization, yielding 250 structural co-word terms). To ensure methodological transparency for the lexical salience scan reported in Section 1.2, an automated Python script scanned the Title and Abstract fields across all 866 included records using the regular-expression dictionary documented in Appendix A (`1 = present`, `0 = absent`). Notably, because VOSviewer indexes author-supplied and database-assigned index keywords in addition to Title/Abstract terms, VOSviewer keyword occurrence counts (e.g., *ego depletion* = 38; *psychological reactance* = 54) are naturally higher than Title/Abstract lexical salience counts ($n = 6$ and $n = 11$, respectively). Full-text two-coder construct coding remains a priority step for future meta-analytic extensions. ### 2.4. ## 3. BIBLIOMETRIC AND THEMATIC RESULTS ### 3.1. Performance Analysis: Publication Trajectories and Leading Outlets Bibliometric performance analysis conducted on our 866 final included studies (2018–2026) reveals a rapid growth trajectory across three distinct developmental phases, visually illustrated in Figure 2: - Foundational Phase (2018–2020): Characterized by exploratory output totaling 34 studies (3.9%; averaging 11.3 publications annually), focusing predominantly on collaborative filtering accuracy and early personalization cues (Shanahan et al., 2019; Xiao & Benbasat, 2018; Zheng et al., 2019). - Expansion Phase (2021–2023): Rapid acceleration totaling 102 studies (11.8%; averaging 34.0 publications annually), catalyzed by the integration of deep neural networks, mobile social commerce, and pandemic-induced digital retail migration (Ampadu et al., 2022; Hallikainen et al., 2022; Redine et al., 2022; Gallin & Portes, 2024; Zhu et al., 2023). - Maturation and Generative Phase (2024–2026): High-velocity scholarly output totaling 730 studies (84.3%; averaging 243.3 publications annually through November 2026), driven by Generative AI, conversational recommender agents, livestreaming curation, and algorithmic dark patterns (Gallin & Portes, 2024; Lin, 2026; Pang et al., 2026; Shamim & Misra, 2025).

### 3.2. Detailed thematic analysis reveals the intellectual core of each cluster: 1. **Cluster 1 (Red): Algorithmic Recommendation Stimuli & System Architecture** - *Core Keywords*: `artificial intelligence`, `recommender system`, `collaborative filtering`, `machine learning`, `perceived personalization`, `algorithmic curation`, `novelty`, `serendipity`. - *Thematic Essence*: This cluster represents the technological foundation of algorithmic commerce. It investigates how predictive architectures translate consumer browsing histories, vector embeddings, and real-time behavioral signals into personalized product feeds (Al-Natour et al., 2011; Ampadu et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2025; Xiao & Benbasat, 2007). Extant studies focus heavily on the trade-off between algorithmic accuracy (precision matching) and serendipity (unexpected discovery), suggesting that excessive accuracy leads to repetitive "filter bubbles" that suppress impulsive exploration, whereas serendipitous and diverse recommendations spark curiosity (Lo et al., 2026; Satinet et al., 2024; Satinet et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b; Xin et al., 2026; Yi et al., 2022; Yin et al., 2025; Gallin & Portes, 2024). 2. **Cluster 2 (Green): Cognitive Organism & Cumulative E-Satisfaction** - *Core Keywords*: `customer satisfaction`, `e-satisfaction`, `trust`, `cognitive fit`, `perceived usefulness`, `cognitive fluency`, `perceived value`. - *Thematic Essence*: Grounded in Cognitive Fit Theory (Vessey, 1991) and Oliver's (1980, 1993) Expectancy-Disconfirmation Model, this cluster examines the cognitive evaluations formed by consumers during algorithmic interactions. When recommendation agents present items that match the user's mental schema with minimal search friction, consumers experience heightened cognitive fluency and operational ease (Florea et al., 2025; Gallin & Portes, 2024; Ngo et al., 2025; Shanahan et al., 2019). This appraisal generates cumulative e-satisfaction (ESAT), establishing institutional trust and lowering perceived transactional risk across omnichannel and sustainability-oriented retail interfaces (Nigam et al., 2022; Sharma & Garg, 2025; Spreng et al., 1996; Yin et al., 2022). 3. **Cluster 3 (Blue): Affective Organism & Impulsive Behavioral Response** - *Core Keywords*: `impulse buying`, `online impulse buying`, `urge to buy impulsively`, `emotional arousal`, `pleasure`, `flow state`, `hedonic consumption`, `spontaneous purchase`. - *Thematic Essence*: Rooted in environmental psychology (Mehrabian & Russell, 1974) and classic impulse buying theory (Beatty & Ferrell, 1998; Rook & Fisher, 1995), this cluster investigates the visceral, emotional reactions triggered by digital shopping environments. Empirical research demonstrates that exposure to dynamic algorithmic feeds, livestreaming cues, and gamified immersive environments induces high-arousal emotional states characterized by heightened excitement, visual absorption, and perceived scarcity (Alawadh & Barnawi, 2025; Feng et al., 2024; Gong & Liu, 2024; Gong et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2025; Lin, 2026; Miranda et al., 2024; Ronda et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026a; Xin et al., 2025; Zhang & Zhang, 2024; Zheng et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2025). This affective surge produces an immediate urge to buy impulsively (UBI), bypassing deliberate price and budget evaluations. 4. **Cluster 4 (Yellow): The Dark Side of Personalization: Algorithmic Surveillance, Privacy Reactance, and Self-Control Fatigue** - *Core Keywords*: `privacy concerns`, `perceived surveillance`, `psychological reactance`, `cognitive dissonance`, `time pressure`, `ego depletion`, `consumer self-control`. - *Thematic Essence*: Crucially, our bibliometric mapping reveals a fourth, highly significant thematic cluster that has been under-examined in prior reviews. This cluster examines the dark side of algorithmic hyper-personalization. When recommendations become excessively invasive, consumers experience the "creepiness factor" or perceived algorithmic surveillance, triggering Brehm's (1966) psychological reactance and skepticism (Komiak & Benbasat, 2006; Kumaran & Shobhana, 2026; Lau et al., 2026; Xiao & Benbasat, 2018). Furthermore, this cluster integrates Baumeister's (2002) Strength Model of Self-Control, showing that prolonged exposure to high-frequency algorithmic nudges induces decision fatigue and ego depletion, temporarily disabling consumer self-regulatory defenses (Baumeister et al., 2007; Kulal et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). ### 3.3. ## 4. CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK AND THEORETICAL PROPOSITIONS ### 4.1. From Generation 1.0 Filtering to Generation 2.0 Generative AI: Dynamic S-O-R Architecture Synthesizing our bibliometric findings and the TCCM empirical matrix, we formulate an integrative Dynamic Dual-Path S-O-R Framework, illustrated in Figure 4. Crucially, to resolve the "AI-specificity disconnect" in prior retail literature, we explicitly distinguish between Algorithmic Generation 1.0 (predictive collaborative filtering and static item feeds, 2011-2021) and Algorithmic Generation 2.0 (Large Language Model conversational assistants, multimodal livestreaming cues, and real-time adaptive agents, 2023-2026). Whereas Generation 1.0 systems passively optimize item matching, Generation 2.0 systems inject social agency, conversational anthropomorphism, and micro-latency persuasion directly into the shopping journey (Huang & Ahmad, 2026; Ma et al., 2026; Pang et al., 2026). As summarized in Table 7, this shift substantially compresses deliberative cognitive latency and heightens cognitive load.

### 4.2. Resolving the Cold-Start Paradox and Endogenous Inverted-U Reactance (P1, P2) A persistent temporal paradox in prior e-commerce literature is the reliance on cumulative e-satisfaction (which requires repeated cross-session transactions) to explain impulsive purchases on algorithmic discovery feeds such as TikTok Shop and Temu, where consumers frequently buy during cold-start first encounters. To reconcile this discrepancy, our framework integrates In-Session Cognitive Fluency (immediate processing ease and instant interface satisfaction) alongside cumulative cross-session e-satisfaction (ESAT) (Gallin & Portes, 2024; Shanahan et al., 2019; Srinivasan et al., 2002). According to Cognitive Fit Theory (Vessey, 1991), when an AI agent delivers information aligned with a consumer's mental schema during an active session, mental search friction drops immediately, generating instant cognitive fluency even without prior platform loyalty. However, rather than assuming a monotonically linear positive effect, we model Perceived Personalization (PP) through an endogenous inverted-U (curvilinear) relationship. Grounded in foundational personalization-privacy paradox research (Awad & Krishnan, 2006; Aguirre et al., 2015) and algorithm appreciation vs. aversion studies (Logg et al., 2019), moderate personalization fosters cognitive fluency and e-satisfaction (Xiao & Benbasat, 2007). Conversely, when algorithmic targeting crosses an intrusive privacy threshold or employs deceptive dark patterns (Mathur et al., 2019), it endogenously triggers Algorithmic Surveillance Reactance within the same consumer (Brehm, 1966; Kumaran & Shobhana, 2026; Lau et al., 2026). Rather than acting purely as an external moderator, surveillance reactance emerges internally from excessive personalization, eroding trust and re-activating deliberative skepticism. Simultaneously, Perceived Recommendation Accuracy (ACC) drives expectancy confirmation (Al-Natour et al., 2011; Oliver, 1980). Therefore, we propose: - **Proposition 1 (P1 - Curvilinear Personalization & Endogenous Surveillance Reactance):** *Perceived personalization exhibits an inverted-U relationship with in-session cognitive fluency and cumulative e-satisfaction, mediated in its downward tail by measurable surveillance reactance once algorithmic specificity crosses privacy, user-control, and transparency thresholds.* - **Proposition 2 (P2):** *Perceived recommendation accuracy positively influences cognitive fluency and e-satisfaction through expectancy confirmation.* ### 4.3. Recommendation Novelty and the Affective Pathway (P3) While accuracy confirms expectations, accuracy alone can result in monotonous, predictable suggestions that fail to generate impulsive excitement. Recommendation Novelty & Serendipity (NOV) (defined as the algorithmic presentation of unexpected yet notably attractive and relevant items; Feng et al., 2024; Lin, 2026) introduces hedonic surprise into the shopping journey. According to Environmental Psychology (Mehrabian & Russell, 1974), unexpected positive environmental stimuli provoke an immediate surge in physiological and emotional arousal. When consumers discover appealing items they did not intentionally search for, hedonic curiosity and pleasure are ignited, producing an immediate affective elevation (Lin, 2026). Therefore, we propose: - **Proposition 3 (P3):** *Recommendation novelty and serendipity positively influence consumer emotional arousal and positive affect.* ### 4.4. Organismic States as the Dual Mediating and Multiplicative Bridge (P4a, P4b, P5, P5a, P5b) In environmental psychology, internal organism states mediate the translation of ambient stimuli into behavioral urges. Traditional consumer decision models position impulse buying as an irrational departure from deliberate calculation (Rook & Fisher, 1995). Through our dual-path lens: 1. The Cognitive Bridge (Cumulative E-Satisfaction): Cumulative e-satisfaction produces a psychological state of affective comfort and disarmed vigilance. When a shopper experiences heightened satisfaction with the algorithmic interface, perceived transaction risk diminishes, cognitive defense mechanisms soften, and trust strengthens (Gallin & Portes, 2024; Oliver, 1993; Spreng et al., 1996). This psychological ease creates an open, receptive mindset that amplifies the spontaneous urge to buy impulsively. 2. The Affective Bridge (Emotional Arousal): Simultaneously, heightened emotional arousal directly stimulates visceral desire. Consumers experiencing hedonic excitement and flow states focus intensely on immediate gratification, diminishing attention to future budgetary constraints (Beatty & Ferrell, 1998; Verhagen & van Dolen, 2011). Thus, cognitive evaluations and emotional arousal do not merely add together linearly; they interact according to the structural equation $UBI = b_1 \text{ESAT} + b_2 \text{Arousal} + b_3 (\text{ESAT} \times \text{Arousal})$. Under the synergistic permission hypothesis ($b_3 > 0$), emotional arousal without cognitive comfort leaves consumers hesitant due to perceived transaction risk, whereas cognitive satisfaction without affective arousal yields deliberate loyalty rather than spontaneous impulse buying (Do Xuan Nguyen & Nguyen, 2026). Conversely, to maximize empirical falsifiability, we specify a competing hot/cool override hypothesis ($b_3 < 0$) grounded in dual-system self-regulation theory (Metcalfe & Mischel, 1999; Hoch & Loewenstein, 1991), whereby extreme visceral ("hot") arousal overwhelms deliberative ("cool") cognitive evaluation even when cognitive satisfaction is low. To resolve the cold-start paradox cleanly, we separate immediate fluency from cumulative e-satisfaction in the propositions below: - **Proposition 4a (P4a - Cold-Start Fluency):** *In-session cognitive fluency positively drives immediate UBI during first-encounter algorithmic browsing without requiring prior platform loyalty.* - **Proposition 4b (P4b - Cumulative E-Satisfaction):** *Cumulative e-satisfaction mediates repeat-session algorithmic stimuli (personalization and accuracy) on UBI by lowering perceived relational risk.* - **Proposition 5 (P5):** *Emotional arousal positively influences the urge to buy impulsively by amplifying visceral hedonic desire.* - **Proposition 5a (P5a - Affective Mediation):** *Emotional arousal mediates the positive relationship between recommendation novelty/serendipity and the urge to buy impulsively.* - **Proposition 5b (P5b - Competing Interaction Hypotheses):** *Cumulative e-satisfaction and emotional arousal interact to shape UBI ($b_3$ in the equation above), with the synergistic permission view predicting positive amplification ($b_3 > 0$) and the competing hot/cool override view predicting affective dominance ($b_3 < 0$).* ### 4.5. The Urge-to-Behavior Transition (P6) The urge to buy impulsively (UBI) represents an acute, felt state of spontaneous desire that precedes transactional execution (Beatty & Ferrell, 1998; Rook & Fisher, 1995). In digital retail environments characterized by frictionless checkout architectures (e.g., Apple Pay, 1-click ordering, saved biometric credentials), the temporal latency between experiencing an impulse and executing payment is compressed to seconds. Extant empirical literature consistently validates that felt impulsive urges represent the most proximate psychological determinant of actual impulse buying behavior (Badgaiyan & Verma, 2015; Zheng et al., 2019). We therefore advance: - **Proposition 6 (P6):** *The urge to buy impulsively positively influences online impulse buying behavior.* ### 4.6. Ego Depletion Boundary Condition (P7a, P7b) and Negative Recursive Feedback Loop (P8) A persistent limitation of static S-O-R models is treating impulsive checkout as a terminal endpoint rather than an ongoing cyclic process. First, grounded in Baumeister's (2002) Strength Model of Self-Control, Vohs and Faber's (2007) experimental demonstration that self-regulatory depletion elevates impulsive spending urges, and Sweller's (1988) Cognitive Load Theory, sustained cognitive exertion can strain executive restraint (Baumeister et al., 2007; Kulal et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). Because large-scale multilab replications report mixed effect sizes for classic depletion tasks (Hagger et al., 2016), we treat self-regulatory strain as a candidate mechanism tested alongside cognitive-load and opportunity-cost controls, acting both as an antecedent to felt urges and as a moderator of checkout execution: - **Proposition 7a (P7a - Urge Elevation):** *Situational self-regulatory strain (ego depletion / cognitive load) positively elevates baseline urge to buy impulsively during high-velocity AI browsing.* - **Proposition 7b (P7b - Checkout Amplification):** *Self-regulatory strain positively moderates the UBI-to-OIB transition, such that impulsive urges convert more readily into unplanned checkout under elevated cognitive fatigue.* Second, we introduce a Negative Recursive Feedback Loop (P8) connecting short-term conversion to long-term platform equity. When platforms exploit ego depletion to trigger unbudgeted purchases, consumers frequently experience post-purchase regret and cognitive dissonance once self-regulatory clarity returns. This negative emotional aftermath erodes cumulative e-satisfaction in subsequent shopping sessions and primes heightened vigilance against future algorithmic surveillance (Kumaran & Shobhana, 2026). Thus: - **Proposition 8 (P8 - Recursive Feedback Loop):** *Online impulse buying executed under high ego depletion induces post-purchase regret, which negatively feeds back to erode future cumulative e-satisfaction and amplify algorithmic surveillance reactance.* ### 4.7. Empirical Operationalization and Model Testing Strategy To translate this theoretical architecture into falsifiable empirical tests without risking model over-parameterization, future quantitative investigations should adopt a two-tier methodological estimation strategy, summarized in Table 8: 1. Latent Quadratic and Multiplicative Structural Estimation (Testing P1 and P5b): Within cross-sectional or experimental designs, researchers should employ Latent Moderated Structural Equations (LMS) or Two-Stage PLS-SEM incorporating explicit quadratic terms ($PP^2$) to test the inverted-U personalization-reactance curve ($P_1$) alongside a multiplicative product indicator ($ESAT \times Arousal$) to validate the permission-kinetic energy interaction ($P_{5b}$), supplemented by Johnson-Neyman floodlight analysis to identify exact ego depletion thresholds ($P_{7a}, P_{7b}$). 2. DISCUSSION, FUTURE RESEARCH AGENDA, AND MANAGERIAL IMPLICATIONS ### 5.1. Theoretical Paradigm Shift: From Static Conversion to Dynamic Algorithmic Well-being Rather than viewing algorithmic retailing through an isolated, static conversion lens, this review repositions consumer impulse buying research from a Static Conversion Optimization Paradigm toward a Dynamic Algorithmic Well-being Paradigm. Our conceptual synthesis makes three integrated advances. First, by contrasting Generation 1.0 collaborative filtering with Generation 2.0 conversational Generative AI (Table 7), we specify how anthropomorphic social agency and micro-latency persuasion compress deliberative evaluation while accelerating cognitive fatigue (Huang & Ahmad, 2026; Pang et al., 2026). Second, we propose that in-session cognitive fluency (P4a) and cumulative e-satisfaction (P4b) operate through separable temporal mechanisms and interact with emotional arousal under competing hypotheses ($b_3 > 0$ synergistic permission vs. $b_3 < 0$ hot/cool override, P5b) (Do Xuan Nguyen & Nguyen, 2026; Hoch & Loewenstein, 1991; Metcalfe & Mischel, 1999). Third, by merging surveillance reactance into an endogenous inverted-U personalization curve ($P_1$), elevating reactance and post-purchase regret to measurable nodes, and framing self-regulatory strain ($P_{7a}, P_{7b}$) alongside cognitive-load and replication debates (Hagger et al., 2016; Sweller, 1988; Vohs & Faber, 2007), we outline how short-term conversion tactics may erode long-term customer trust. ### 5.2. Managerial and Ethical Implications: Tiered "Ethical Friction" for Sustainable CLV For retail executives and algorithm architects, our dynamic model elevates ethical design from mere legal compliance to a core Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) retention strategy: - Calibrating the March (1991) Exploitation-Exploration Ratio: Drawing on James March's (1991) organizational learning paradigm, platforms must balance *exploitation* (high-accuracy matching) with *exploration* (serendipitous discovery) to stimulate curiosity without crossing the inverted-U surveillance threshold (Li et al., 2025). - Tiered "Ethical Friction" Architecture and Regulatory Alignment: Rather than applying blanket checkout delays that harm user experience, platforms should evaluate tiered ethical friction calibrated by product regret risk, aligning interface design with binding statutory mandates under the European Union Digital Services Act (DSA) (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, Article 25 prohibiting deceptive dark patterns; European Parliament and Council, 2022) and the U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Staff Report on digital dark patterns (Federal Trade Commission, 2022; Mathur et al., 2019). For *low-regret, low-ticket consumables*, frictionless checkout preserves convenience. Conversely, for *high-regret, high-involvement discretionary items* encountered during late-night sessions or rapid browsing streaks indicative of cognitive strain, platforms should test smart cooling-off nudges, transparent recommendation rationales ("*Why am I seeing this?*"), and optional 24-hour cart locks (Tobon & Abril, 2024). Crucially, these interventions must be validated through randomized A/B field trials that jointly measure short-term conversion, post-purchase return rates, and long-term Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) before platform-wide rollout. ### 5.3. An Actionable 5-Pillar Future Research Agenda To guide scholarship over the coming decade, we articulate a structured 5-Pillar Future Research Agenda, accompanied by explicit empirical research questions in Table 9: 1. **Pillar 1: Methodological Triangulation (fsQCA and Necessary Condition Analysis - NCA)**: Extant scholarship relies heavily on linear, symmetrical regression techniques (CB-SEM, PLS-SEM). Future research must embrace causal complexity through fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) and NCA to identify asymmetric configurations of algorithmic stimuli that are necessary or sufficient for high impulse conversion. 2. **Pillar 2: Experimental Ego Depletion and Real-Time Cognitive Load Manipulation**: Rather than relying on self-reported trait self-control scales, experimental consumer researchers should deploy dual-task laboratory manipulations (e.g., Stroop color-word interference, cognitive load memory burdens) to causally test the depletion boundary condition under varying algorithmic interface speeds. 3. **Pillar 3: Neuromarketing and Physiological Telemetry**: Integrate multi-modal neuro-physiological measurements, such as eye-tracking gaze fixation, pupillometry (arousal index), galvanic skin response (GSR), and facial expression analysis, to capture non-conscious affective arousal during live recommendation scrolling. 4. **Pillar 4: Ethical Algorithmic Guardrails, Dark Patterns, and Consumer Cooling-Off Mechanics**: Investigate how platform-enforced ethical guardrails (e.g., algorithmic nutrition labels, voluntary spending friction) impact consumer trust, perceived paternalism, and long-term customer lifetime value versus short-term impulse revenue. 5. **Pillar 5: Generative AI, Conversational Agents, and Cross-Cultural Longitudinal Designs**: Examine how conversational LLM shopping agents substantially alter social presence and anthropomorphic trust (Huang & Ahmad, 2026; Ma et al., 2026). Furthermore, deploy longitudinal latent growth curve modeling across Western and Eastern e-commerce platforms to capture temporal changes in algorithmic tolerance.

### 5.4. Limitations and Conclusion In accordance with the PRISMA 2020 reporting standard (Item 23c; Page et al., 2021), several methodological boundaries of this review warrant transparent acknowledgment. First, this review focuses on the Dimensions database to leverage its comprehensive interdisciplinary coverage of peer-reviewed research bridging artificial intelligence and electronic commerce (Thelwall, 2018; Visser et al., 2021). Future reviews may cross-validate these patterns against Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection where institutional access permits. Second, our exclusion of non-journal and non-peer-reviewed outlets (EC1: preprints, monographs, edited books, grants, and conference proceedings) omits leading computer science venues such as ACM RecSys, KDD, SIGIR, and CHI, where early Generative AI recommendation architectures frequently debut prior to journal publication. Third, restricting inclusion to English-language outlets (IC1) may underrepresent regional innovations in live-streaming social commerce originating in East Asian markets. Fourth, because the underlying empirical corpus relies heavily on self-reported cross-sectional surveys rather than longitudinal behavioral telemetry, causal inferences regarding temporal feedback dynamics ($P_8$) require formal panel validation. Notwithstanding these limitations, this study advances international retailing scholarship by integrating PRISMA 2020 screening ($N = 866$), quantitative VOSviewer science mapping across four thematic clusters, and a Dynamic and Multiplicative Dual-Path S-O-R Framework. By theorizing how algorithmic Generation 2.0 agents interact with in-session cognitive fluency, affective kinetic energy, inverted-U surveillance reactance, and ego depletion regret loops, this review # Algorithmic Persuasion, Cognitive Depletion, and Online Impulse Buying: A Systematic Review and Dynamic Dual-Path S-O-R Framework (2018-2026) **Author:** Le Phuc Hai (Lê Phúc Hải) **Affiliation:** NCSKIT.org (Independent Research Group) **ORCID:** [https://orcid.org/0009-0004-1215-5023](https://orcid.org/0009-0004-1215-5023) **Correspondence:** [hailp@ncskit.org](mailto:hailp@ncskit.org) --- ## HIGHLIGHTS - Synthesizes 866 studies on AI recommenders and impulse buying (2018-2026). - Uncovers four clusters via VOSviewer, with Dark Side newest (APY = 2024.4). - Separates cold-start fluency from cumulative e-satisfaction (P4a-P4b). - Contrasts competing cognitive-affective interactions (b3 > 0 vs. b3 < 0). - Links tiered ethical friction to EU DSA/FTC principles and A/B trials. --- ## ABSTRACT The rapid deployment of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered personalized recommendation systems across digital retailing platforms has substantially altered consumer browsing dynamics, shifting electronic commerce from deliberate keyword-driven search toward algorithmically curated discovery. While practitioners deploy predictive and generative algorithms to stimulate conversion, academic inquiry into the cognitive-affective mechanics governing AI-mediated impulsive consumption remains theoretically fragmented. Following PRISMA 2020 reporting principles and the TCCM framework, this study conducts a systematic literature review and bibliometric science mapping on 2,458 initial records retrieved from the Dimensions scholarly database (January 2018 to November 2026), retaining peer-reviewed journal articles with valid DOIs after excluding preprints, books, monographs, and grants. After deduplication (1,441 unique records) and two-stage eligibility screening, 866 focal studies were mapped in VOSviewer. Bibliometric mapping reveals four thematic clusters: (1) Algorithmic Recommendation Stimuli (Cluster 1 - Red); (2) Cognitive Organism and E-Satisfaction (Cluster 2 - Green); (3) Affective Organism and Impulsive Behavioral Response (Cluster 3 - Blue); and (4) The Dark Side of Personalization: Algorithmic Surveillance, Privacy Reactance, and Self-Control Fatigue (Cluster 4 - Yellow), which emerges as the most recent research frontier (mean $\text{APY} = 2024.4$). Advancing beyond static additive S-O-R models, we formulate a Dynamic Dual-Path S-O-R Framework contrasting Generation 1.0 collaborative filtering with Generation 2.0 conversational Generative AI. We separate in-session cognitive fluency (cold-start) from cumulative e-satisfaction (repeat sessions) and specify competing interaction hypotheses ($b_3 > 0$ synergistic permission vs. $b_3 < 0$ hot/cool override). We further integrate endogenous surveillance reactance (P1), candidate self-regulatory strain (P7a/P7b), and a recursive post-purchase regret loop (P8), concluding with a 5-pillar research agenda and regulatory-aligned A/B testing propositions. **Keywords**: Artificial Intelligence; Personalized Recommendation Systems; Online Impulse Buying; Dual-Path S-O-R Model; PRISMA 2020; VOSviewer Bibliometrics; Cognitive Fit Theory; Ego Depletion; Algorithmic Dark Patterns. --- ## 1. INTRODUCTION ### 1.1. Background and The Algorithmic Retailing Paradigm Shift In contemporary digital retailing ecosystems, consumers no longer navigate static, hierarchical category trees (Shanahan et al., 2019; Xiao & Benbasat, 2018). Instead, they are continuously enveloped within dynamic, hyper-personalized information streams driven by deep neural collaborative filtering, transformer-based sequential recommenders, and real-time behavioral telemetry (Al-Natour et al., 2011; Hallikainen et al., 2022). The foundational architecture of consumer discovery has shifted from deliberative, keyword-driven item retrieval (*search-based shopping*) to serendipitous, algorithmically triggered consumption (*discovery-based shopping*) (Sundar & Kim, 2019; Wang et al., 2022). Building on foundational digital retailing frameworks (Dwivedi et al., 2021; Guha et al., 2021), the proliferation of Large Language Model (LLM)-powered conversational shopping agents and Generative AI interfaces between 2023 and 2026 (Do Xuan Nguyen & Nguyen, 2026; Huang & Ahmad, 2026; Pang et al., 2026) enables platforms to anticipate and shape latent consumer desires in real time. A primary behavioral outcome of this algorithmic immersion is online impulse buying (OIB) (defined as sudden, hedonically complex, and unplanned purchase decisions characterized by diminished deliberative cognitive evaluation) (Beatty & Ferrell, 1998; Rook & Fisher, 1995). Prior systematic reviews establish that unplanned purchasing constitutes a substantial share of digital commerce activity, catalyzed by algorithmic discovery feeds, flash recommendations, and frictionless one-click checkout infrastructures (Chan et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2019). While practitioners celebrate predictive personalization as an engine of customer lifetime value and transaction velocity, consumer psychologists express growing scholarly concern regarding the ethical boundaries of algorithmic nudging, choice architecture manipulation, and the erosion of consumer self-regulatory willpower (Baumeister, 2002; Kumaran & Shobhana, 2026; Sweller, 1988). ### 1.2. Problem Statement, Salience Audit, and Positioning Relative to Prior Reviews Despite substantial growth in empirical scholarship over the past decade, literature examining the nexus of AI recommendation systems and impulsive buying remains siloed across computer science, information systems (IS), and consumer psychology. A preliminary lexical salience scan of Title and Abstract fields across our 866-study corpus indicates that while 12.01% ($n = 104$) of abstracts explicitly invoke S-O-R framing, explicit Title/Abstract mentions of interaction or moderated-mediation terms (2.19%, $n = 19$), curvilinear or threshold terms (1.50%, $n = 13$), surveillance, reactance, or privacy-paradox terms (1.27%, $n = 11$), regret, dissonance, or product-return terms (3.58%, $n = 31$), and ego-depletion or decision-fatigue terms (0.69%, $n = 6$) remain sparse. As detailed in Section 2.3 and Appendix A, these Title/Abstract counts represent conservative lower bounds of lexical salience relative to full-corpus author/index keyword occurrences. Three core theoretical fault lines motivate our synthesis: 1. Theoretical Fragmentation of Algorithmic Stimuli (The S-O-R Disconnect): While the classical Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) paradigm (Mehrabian & Russell, 1974; Jacoby, 2002) provides an established environmental psychology foundation, early retail studies operationalized "Stimuli" primarily as static website atmospherics (e.g., color, layout, navigation structure; Eroglu et al., 2001). In algorithmic commerce, stimuli are dynamic, adaptive, and agentic. Crucially, literature exhibits sharp disagreement on whether algorithmic attributes, specifically *Perceived Personalization (PP)*, *Perceived Recommendation Accuracy (ACC)*, and *Recommendation Novelty & Serendipity (NOV)*, operate harmoniously or create conflicting psychological appraisals (Al-Natour et al., 2011; Ampadu et al., 2022; Gallin & Portes, 2024; Shanahan et al., 2019). 2. The Dual-Path Cognitive-Affective Divide (The Organismic Black Box): Existing literature often treats internal consumer organismic states as a monolithic construct. While some scholars emphasize cognitive evaluations like cumulative e-satisfaction (ESAT) (Oliver, 1980, 1993; Spreng et al., 1996), others argue that impulse buying is primarily an affective, visceral response driven by emotional arousal and hedonic flow (Beatty & Ferrell, 1998; Verhagen & van Dolen, 2011). Extant research has yet to fully reconcile how cumulative satisfaction interacts with immediate cold-start fluency and visceral urges, or when over-personalization induces perceived algorithmic surveillance and reactance (Komiak & Benbasat, 2006; Xiao & Benbasat, 2007, 2018). 3. The Intention-Behavior Gap and Self-Regulatory Boundaries: Traditional marketing models frequently conflate the psychological *urge to buy impulsively (UBI)* with the enacted *online impulse buying behavior (OIB)*. However, empirical consumer psychology demonstrates that an impulse urge does not inevitably result in transactional checkout (Badgaiyan & Verma, 2015; Rook & Fisher, 1995). Candidate self-regulatory mechanisms, including resource depletion (Baumeister, 2002; Baumeister et al., 2007; Vohs & Faber, 2007) alongside cognitive load theory (Sweller, 1988) and multilab replication debates (Hagger et al., 2016), require careful integration into dynamic models of algorithmic retailing. To clarify incremental positioning, Table 1 contrasts this review against prior landmark reviews and temporal S-O-R models (Chan et al., 2017; Mariani et al., 2022; Tobon & Abril, 2024; Kumaran & Shobhana, 2026). **Table 1: Positioning Against Prior Landmark Reviews and Temporal S-O-R Models** | Study | Scope & Corpus | Curvilinear Privacy / Reactance | Fluency vs. Cumulative ESAT | Competing Interaction ($b_3$) | Recursive Regret Loop | | :--- | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | | **Chan et al. (2017)** | Pre-AI online impulse buying SLR | No | No | No | No | | **Mariani et al. (2022)** | Broad AI in marketing & psychology SLR | Partial (Ethics) | No | No | No | | **Tobon & Abril (2024)** | Apparel e-tailer impulse & returns | No | No | No | Yes (Returns) | | **Kumaran & Shobhana (2026)** | GenAI synthetic urgency & regret | Yes (Urgency) | No | No | Partial | | **Current Study (2026)** | 866-study AI-impulse SLR + Dual-Path Agenda | Yes (Endogenous P1) | Yes (P4a vs. P4b) | Yes ($b_3 > 0$ vs. $b_3 < 0$) | Yes (P8 + ESM) | ### 1.3. Research Objectives and Formal Research Questions To resolve these theoretical fault lines, this study executes an integrative multi-method investigation combining the PRISMA 2020 systematic review protocol with VOSviewer science mapping and the TCCM synthesis framework. Specifically, we address three overarching research questions: - **RQ1**: *What is the intellectual structure, thematic cluster architecture, and temporal evolution of international scholarship investigating AI recommendation systems and online impulse buying?* - **RQ2**: *Through what dual-path cognitive-affective mechanisms do algorithmic stimuli influence consumer organismic states, and how do these states mediate the translation into impulsive purchasing urges and behaviors?* - **RQ3**: *What psychological and technological boundary conditions govern this translation, and what future research agenda and ethical guardrails are necessary for sustainable algorithmic retailing?* ### 1.4. Paper Structure The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 delineates the systematic review methodology, detailing the PRISMA 2020 protocol, search strings, TCCM framing, text-mining gap audit protocol, and VOSviewer co-occurrence parameters. Section 3 presents the bibliometric performance analysis, VOSviewer quantitative cluster metrics and science mapping, and the TCCM empirical synthesis matrix. Section 4 articulates the integrative conceptual framework, develops eight core theoretical propositions (P1-P8, encompassing cold-start vs. cumulative paths P4a/P4b, affective mediation P5a, competing interaction P5b, and regulatory strain P7a/P7b), and outlines an empirical testing strategy. Section 5 discusses theoretical contributions, tiered ethical friction implications, details the 5-pillar future research agenda, acknowledges study limitations, and concludes. ## 2. METHODOLOGY: THE PRISMA 2020 PROTOCOL AND BIBLIOMETRIC DESIGN ### 2.1. Methodological Design and Agnostic Search Strategy To prevent confirmation bias, the identification strategy adhered to an agnostic three-block Boolean structure covering technological stimuli (AI recommendation engines), behavioral outcomes (impulse purchasing), and digital retail contexts. Theoretical frameworks (such as S-O-R) and mediating constructs (such as e-satisfaction) were intentionally excluded from search strings so thematic clusters emerged inductively (Paul & Criado, 2020). Searches were executed on November 15, 2026 in the Dimensions scholarly database (`title_abstract` / full-data indexing), selected for its extensive coverage of interdisciplinary research across artificial intelligence, data science, and applied digital commerce. Large-scale bibliometric benchmarks by Thelwall (2018) and Visser et al. (2021) demonstrate that Dimensions achieves publication coverage comparable to, and in technology and applied computing domains often broader than, Scopus and Web of Science. Because Dimensions indexes diverse document types, rigorous programmatic filtering was applied to isolate peer-reviewed journal articles with valid Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs). The standardized conceptual Boolean query is shown below: ```text TITLE-ABS-KEY ( ( "artificial intelligence" OR "AI" OR "recommendation system*" OR "recommender system*" OR "algorithmic recommendation*" OR "personalized recommendation*" OR "deep learning recommendation*" OR "collaborative filtering" ) AND ( "impulse buying" OR "impulsive buying" OR "impulse purchase*" OR "spontaneous purchase*" OR "unplanned purchase*" OR "urge to buy impulsively" ) AND ( "e-commerce" OR "online shopping" OR "digital retailing" OR "electronic commerce" OR "social commerce" OR "mobile commerce" ) ) ``` ### 2.2. Eligibility Criteria and TCCM Framework Framing The screening protocol was framed around the TCCM Framework (Theory, Context, Characteristics, Methodology), recognized as a widely adopted framework for systematic reviews in marketing and retailing (Paul & Rosado-Serrano, 2019; Paul & Criado, 2020): - Theory (T): Studies examining behavioral, psychological, or information processing mechanisms (e.g., S-O-R, Cognitive Fit Theory, Dual-Process Theory, Self-Regulation). - Context (C): Digital retailing environments including electronic commerce, mobile retailing, social commerce, and livestream shopping platforms. - Characteristics (C): Algorithmic system attributes (personalization, accuracy, novelty, transparency) and consumer internal states (fluency, e-satisfaction, arousal, urge). - Methodology (M): Rigorous empirical investigations (laboratory experiments, field surveys, neuro-marketing, structural equation modeling, fsQCA) alongside foundational conceptual and systematic review benchmarks that establish core construct taxonomies. We established four explicit Inclusion Criteria (IC) and four Exclusion Criteria (EC): - **IC1**: Published in English in peer-reviewed scholarly journals between January 2018 and November 2026. - **IC2**: Empirical investigation or foundational conceptual/review benchmark explicitly analyzing AI/algorithmic recommendation features and consumer impulse buying dynamics. - **IC3**: For empirical studies, clear reporting of sample size, analytical technique, and theoretical grounding (foundational conceptual/review benchmarks retained under IC2 are exempted from sample-size reporting). - **IC4**: Indexed in Dimensions as a peer-reviewed journal article (`type = article`) carrying a valid, resolvable DOI. - **EC1**: Non-peer-reviewed and non-journal Dimensions records, including all Preprints, Monographs, Edited Books, Grants, editorials, commentaries, and conference abstracts. - **EC2**: Purely algorithmic optimization studies focusing solely on matrix factorization or loss function mathematics without measuring human behavioral responses. - **EC3**: Studies situated purely in brick-and-mortar physical stores with no digital recommendation interface. - **EC4**: Duplicate records across databases. ### 2.3. The 4-Stage Screening Funnel (2,458 to 866 Articles) Adhering to the PRISMA 2020 statement (Page et al., 2021), the data collection and screening process progressed through four transparent, auditable stages: 1. Identification: Database retrieval from Dimensions yielded 2,458 initial records after applying document-type restrictions (excluding grants, monographs, edited books, and preprints) to retain peer-reviewed journal candidates with valid DOIs. 2. Deduplication: Using R `bibliometrix` and a custom Python reconciliation script, 1,017 duplicate records were programmatically identified and removed using normalized DOI and title-Levenshtein distance matching, yielding 1,441 unique records entering the screening stage. 3. Screening (Title & Abstract): Two independent research assistants conducted blind title and abstract screening against IC1-IC4 and EC1-EC3, with the author serving as the senior third adjudicator. Inter-coder reliability was strong (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.89$; PABAK = 0.91). Disagreements on 34 articles at the Title/Abstract stage (and 18 marginal papers at the subsequent Full-Text stage) were adjudicated by the senior third reviewer, resulting in the exclusion of 496 irrelevant records (primarily technical benchmarking papers without human behavioral data), leaving 945 full-text articles. 4. Eligibility & Final Inclusion: All 945 full-text articles were evaluated in depth ($\kappa_{\text{FT}} = 0.87$), with 18 marginal cases resolved by the senior third reviewer (complementing the 34 Title/Abstract adjudications above). Of these, 79 articles were excluded due to incomplete empirical metrics ($n = 45$; e.g., missing sample sizes or reliability/validity indicators in empirical designs, while retaining foundational conceptual/review benchmarks under IC2) or lacking explicit impulse buying construct measures ($n = 34$). The final systematic synthesis and science mapping corpus comprises 866 peer-reviewed articles (within which a strict 3-pillar empirical core of $n = 167$ studies is flagged in the OSF screening ledger alongside the broader thematic corpus). All 866 studies were analyzed in VOSviewer using keyword co-occurrence network analysis ($T \ge 5$ occurrences, full counting with association strength normalization, yielding 250 structural co-word terms). To ensure methodological transparency for the lexical salience scan reported in Section 1.2, an automated Python script scanned the Title and Abstract fields across all 866 included records using the regular-expression dictionary documented in Appendix A (`1 = present`, `0 = absent`). Notably, because VOSviewer indexes author-supplied and database-assigned index keywords in addition to Title/Abstract terms, VOSviewer keyword occurrence counts (e.g., *ego depletion* = 38; *psychological reactance* = 54) are naturally higher than Title/Abstract lexical salience counts ($n = 6$ and $n = 11$, respectively). Full-text two-coder construct coding remains a priority step for future meta-analytic extensions. ### 2.4. Detailed thematic analysis reveals the intellectual core of each cluster: 1. **Cluster 1 (Red): Algorithmic Recommendation Stimuli & System Architecture** - *Core Keywords*: `artificial intelligence`, `recommender system`, `collaborative filtering`, `machine learning`, `perceived personalization`, `algorithmic curation`, `novelty`, `serendipity`. - *Thematic Essence*: This cluster represents the technological foundation of algorithmic commerce. It investigates how predictive architectures translate consumer browsing histories, vector embeddings, and real-time behavioral signals into personalized product feeds (Al-Natour et al., 2011; Ampadu et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2025; Xiao & Benbasat, 2007). Extant studies focus heavily on the trade-off between algorithmic accuracy (precision matching) and serendipity (unexpected discovery), suggesting that excessive accuracy leads to repetitive "filter bubbles" that suppress impulsive exploration, whereas serendipitous and diverse recommendations spark curiosity (Lo et al., 2026; Satinet et al., 2024; Satinet et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b; Xin et al., 2026; Yi et al., 2022; Yin et al., 2025; Gallin & Portes, 2024). 2. **Cluster 2 (Green): Cognitive Organism & Cumulative E-Satisfaction** - *Core Keywords*: `customer satisfaction`, `e-satisfaction`, `trust`, `cognitive fit`, `perceived usefulness`, `cognitive fluency`, `perceived value`. - *Thematic Essence*: Grounded in Cognitive Fit Theory (Vessey, 1991) and Oliver's (1980, 1993) Expectancy-Disconfirmation Model, this cluster examines the cognitive evaluations formed by consumers during algorithmic interactions. When recommendation agents present items that match the user's mental schema with minimal search friction, consumers experience heightened cognitive fluency and operational ease (Florea et al., 2025; Gallin & Portes, 2024; Ngo et al., 2025; Shanahan et al., 2019). This appraisal generates cumulative e-satisfaction (ESAT), establishing institutional trust and lowering perceived transactional risk across omnichannel and sustainability-oriented retail interfaces (Nigam et al., 2022; Sharma & Garg, 2025; Spreng et al., 1996; Yin et al., 2022). 3. **Cluster 3 (Blue): Affective Organism & Impulsive Behavioral Response** - *Core Keywords*: `impulse buying`, `online impulse buying`, `urge to buy impulsively`, `emotional arousal`, `pleasure`, `flow state`, `hedonic consumption`, `spontaneous purchase`. - *Thematic Essence*: Rooted in environmental psychology (Mehrabian & Russell, 1974) and classic impulse buying theory (Beatty & Ferrell, 1998; Rook & Fisher, 1995), this cluster investigates the visceral, emotional reactions triggered by digital shopping environments. Empirical research demonstrates that exposure to dynamic algorithmic feeds, livestreaming cues, and gamified immersive environments induces high-arousal emotional states characterized by heightened excitement, visual absorption, and perceived scarcity (Alawadh & Barnawi, 2025; Feng et al., 2024; Gong & Liu, 2024; Gong et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2025; Lin, 2026; Miranda et al., 2024; Ronda et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026a; Xin et al., 2025; Zhang & Zhang, 2024; Zheng et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2025). This affective surge produces an immediate urge to buy impulsively (UBI), bypassing deliberate price and budget evaluations. 4. **Cluster 4 (Yellow): The Dark Side of Personalization: Algorithmic Surveillance, Privacy Reactance, and Self-Control Fatigue** - *Core Keywords*: `privacy concerns`, `perceived surveillance`, `psychological reactance`, `cognitive dissonance`, `time pressure`, `ego depletion`, `consumer self-control`. - *Thematic Essence*: Crucially, our bibliometric mapping reveals a fourth, highly significant thematic cluster that has been under-examined in prior reviews. This cluster examines the dark side of algorithmic hyper-personalization. When recommendations become excessively invasive, consumers experience the "creepiness factor" or perceived algorithmic surveillance, triggering Brehm's (1966) psychological reactance and skepticism (Komiak & Benbasat, 2006; Kumaran & Shobhana, 2026; Lau et al., 2026; Xiao & Benbasat, 2018). Furthermore, this cluster integrates Baumeister's (2002) Strength Model of Self-Control, showing that prolonged exposure to high-frequency algorithmic nudges induces decision fatigue and ego depletion, temporarily disabling consumer self-regulatory defenses (Baumeister et al., 2007; Kulal et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). ### 3.3. ## 4. CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK AND THEORETICAL PROPOSITIONS ### 4.1. From Generation 1.0 Filtering to Generation 2.0 Generative AI: Dynamic S-O-R Architecture Synthesizing our bibliometric findings and the TCCM empirical matrix, we formulate an integrative Dynamic Dual-Path S-O-R Framework, illustrated in Figure 4. Crucially, to resolve the "AI-specificity disconnect" in prior retail literature, we explicitly distinguish between Algorithmic Generation 1.0 (predictive collaborative filtering and static item feeds, 2011-2021) and Algorithmic Generation 2.0 (Large Language Model conversational assistants, multimodal livestreaming cues, and real-time adaptive agents, 2023-2026). Whereas Generation 1.0 systems passively optimize item matching, Generation 2.0 systems inject social agency, conversational anthropomorphism, and micro-latency persuasion directly into the shopping journey (Huang & Ahmad, 2026; Ma et al., 2026; Pang et al., 2026). ### 4.2. Resolving the Cold-Start Paradox and Endogenous Inverted-U Reactance (P1, P2) A persistent temporal paradox in prior e-commerce literature is the reliance on cumulative e-satisfaction (which requires repeated cross-session transactions) to explain impulsive purchases on algorithmic discovery feeds such as TikTok Shop and Temu, where consumers frequently buy during cold-start first encounters. To reconcile this discrepancy, our framework integrates In-Session Cognitive Fluency (immediate processing ease and instant interface satisfaction) alongside cumulative cross-session e-satisfaction (ESAT) (Gallin & Portes, 2024; Shanahan et al., 2019; Srinivasan et al., 2002). According to Cognitive Fit Theory (Vessey, 1991), when an AI agent delivers information aligned with a consumer's mental schema during an active session, mental search friction drops immediately, generating instant cognitive fluency even without prior platform loyalty. However, rather than assuming a monotonically linear positive effect, we model Perceived Personalization (PP) through an endogenous inverted-U (curvilinear) relationship. Grounded in foundational personalization-privacy paradox research (Awad & Krishnan, 2006; Aguirre et al., 2015) and algorithm appreciation vs. aversion studies (Logg et al., 2019), moderate personalization fosters cognitive fluency and e-satisfaction (Xiao & Benbasat, 2007). Conversely, when algorithmic targeting crosses an intrusive privacy threshold or employs deceptive dark patterns (Mathur et al., 2019), it endogenously triggers Algorithmic Surveillance Reactance within the same consumer (Brehm, 1966; Kumaran & Shobhana, 2026; Lau et al., 2026). Rather than acting purely as an external moderator, surveillance reactance emerges internally from excessive personalization, eroding trust and re-activating deliberative skepticism. Simultaneously, Perceived Recommendation Accuracy (ACC) drives expectancy confirmation (Al-Natour et al., 2011; Oliver, 1980). Therefore, we propose: - **Proposition 1 (P1 - Curvilinear Personalization & Endogenous Surveillance Reactance):** *Perceived personalization exhibits an inverted-U relationship with in-session cognitive fluency and cumulative e-satisfaction, mediated in its downward tail by measurable surveillance reactance once algorithmic specificity crosses privacy, user-control, and transparency thresholds.* - **Proposition 2 (P2):** *Perceived recommendation accuracy positively influences cognitive fluency and e-satisfaction through expectancy confirmation.* ### 4.3. Recommendation Novelty and the Affective Pathway (P3) While accuracy confirms expectations, accuracy alone can result in monotonous, predictable suggestions that fail to generate impulsive excitement. Recommendation Novelty & Serendipity (NOV) (defined as the algorithmic presentation of unexpected yet notably attractive and relevant items; Feng et al., 2024; Lin, 2026) introduces hedonic surprise into the shopping journey. According to Environmental Psychology (Mehrabian & Russell, 1974), unexpected positive environmental stimuli provoke an immediate surge in physiological and emotional arousal. When consumers discover appealing items they did not intentionally search for, hedonic curiosity and pleasure are ignited, producing an immediate affective elevation (Lin, 2026). Therefore, we propose: - **Proposition 3 (P3):** *Recommendation novelty and serendipity positively influence consumer emotional arousal and positive affect.* ### 4.4. Organismic States as the Dual Mediating and Multiplicative Bridge (P4a, P4b, P5, P5a, P5b) In environmental psychology, internal organism states mediate the translation of ambient stimuli into behavioral urges. Traditional consumer decision models position impulse buying as an irrational departure from deliberate calculation (Rook & Fisher, 1995). Through our dual-path lens: 1. The Cognitive Bridge (Cumulative E-Satisfaction): Cumulative e-satisfaction produces a psychological state of affective comfort and disarmed vigilance. When a shopper experiences heightened satisfaction with the algorithmic interface, perceived transaction risk diminishes, cognitive defense mechanisms soften, and trust strengthens (Gallin & Portes, 2024; Oliver, 1993; Spreng et al., 1996). This psychological ease creates an open, receptive mindset that amplifies the spontaneous urge to buy impulsively. 2. The Affective Bridge (Emotional Arousal): Simultaneously, heightened emotional arousal directly stimulates visceral desire. Consumers experiencing hedonic excitement and flow states focus intensely on immediate gratification, diminishing attention to future budgetary constraints (Beatty & Ferrell, 1998; Verhagen & van Dolen, 2011). Thus, cognitive evaluations and emotional arousal do not merely add together linearly; they interact according to the structural equation $UBI = b_1 \text{ESAT} + b_2 \text{Arousal} + b_3 (\text{ESAT} \times \text{Arousal})$. Under the synergistic permission hypothesis ($b_3 > 0$), emotional arousal without cognitive comfort leaves consumers hesitant due to perceived transaction risk, whereas cognitive satisfaction without affective arousal yields deliberate loyalty rather than spontaneous impulse buying (Do Xuan Nguyen & Nguyen, 2026). Conversely, to maximize empirical falsifiability, we specify a competing hot/cool override hypothesis ($b_3 < 0$) grounded in dual-system self-regulation theory (Metcalfe & Mischel, 1999; Hoch & Loewenstein, 1991), whereby extreme visceral ("hot") arousal overwhelms deliberative ("cool") cognitive evaluation even when cognitive satisfaction is low. To resolve the cold-start paradox cleanly, we separate immediate fluency from cumulative e-satisfaction in the propositions below: - **Proposition 4a (P4a - Cold-Start Fluency):** *In-session cognitive fluency positively drives immediate UBI during first-encounter algorithmic browsing without requiring prior platform loyalty.* - **Proposition 4b (P4b - Cumulative E-Satisfaction):** *Cumulative e-satisfaction mediates repeat-session algorithmic stimuli (personalization and accuracy) on UBI by lowering perceived relational risk.* - **Proposition 5 (P5):** *Emotional arousal positively influences the urge to buy impulsively by amplifying visceral hedonic desire.* - **Proposition 5a (P5a - Affective Mediation):** *Emotional arousal mediates the positive relationship between recommendation novelty/serendipity and the urge to buy impulsively.* - **Proposition 5b (P5b - Competing Interaction Hypotheses):** *Cumulative e-satisfaction and emotional arousal interact to shape UBI ($b_3$ in the equation above), with the synergistic permission view predicting positive amplification ($b_3 > 0$) and the competing hot/cool override view predicting affective dominance ($b_3 < 0$).* ### 4.5. The Urge-to-Behavior Transition (P6) The urge to buy impulsively (UBI) represents an acute, felt state of spontaneous desire that precedes transactional execution (Beatty & Ferrell, 1998; Rook & Fisher, 1995). In digital retail environments characterized by frictionless checkout architectures (e.g., Apple Pay, 1-click ordering, saved biometric credentials), the temporal latency between experiencing an impulse and executing payment is compressed to seconds. Extant empirical literature consistently validates that felt impulsive urges represent the most proximate psychological determinant of actual impulse buying behavior (Badgaiyan & Verma, 2015; Zheng et al., 2019). We therefore advance: - **Proposition 6 (P6):** *The urge to buy impulsively positively influences online impulse buying behavior.* ### 4.6. Ego Depletion Boundary Condition (P7a, P7b) and Negative Recursive Feedback Loop (P8) A persistent limitation of static S-O-R models is treating impulsive checkout as a terminal endpoint rather than an ongoing cyclic process. First, grounded in Baumeister's (2002) Strength Model of Self-Control, Vohs and Faber's (2007) experimental demonstration that self-regulatory depletion elevates impulsive spending urges, and Sweller's (1988) Cognitive Load Theory, sustained cognitive exertion can strain executive restraint (Baumeister et al., 2007; Kulal et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). Because large-scale multilab replications report mixed effect sizes for classic depletion tasks (Hagger et al., 2016), we treat self-regulatory strain as a candidate mechanism tested alongside cognitive-load and opportunity-cost controls, acting both as an antecedent to felt urges and as a moderator of checkout execution: - **Proposition 7a (P7a - Urge Elevation):** *Situational self-regulatory strain (ego depletion / cognitive load) positively elevates baseline urge to buy impulsively during high-velocity AI browsing.* - **Proposition 7b (P7b - Checkout Amplification):** *Self-regulatory strain positively moderates the UBI-to-OIB transition, such that impulsive urges convert more readily into unplanned checkout under elevated cognitive fatigue.* Second, we introduce a Negative Recursive Feedback Loop (P8) connecting short-term conversion to long-term platform equity. When platforms exploit ego depletion to trigger unbudgeted purchases, consumers frequently experience post-purchase regret and cognitive dissonance once self-regulatory clarity returns. This negative emotional aftermath erodes cumulative e-satisfaction in subsequent shopping sessions and primes heightened vigilance against future algorithmic surveillance (Kumaran & Shobhana, 2026). Thus: - **Proposition 8 (P8 - Recursive Feedback Loop):** *Online impulse buying executed under high ego depletion induces post-purchase regret, which negatively feeds back to erode future cumulative e-satisfaction and amplify algorithmic surveillance reactance.* ### 4.7. Empirical Operationalization and Model Testing Strategy To translate this theoretical architecture into falsifiable empirical tests without risking model over-parameterization, future quantitative investigations should adopt a two-tier methodological estimation strategy, summarized in Table 8: 1. Latent Quadratic and Multiplicative Structural Estimation (Testing P1 and P5b): Within cross-sectional or experimental designs, researchers should employ Latent Moderated Structural Equations (LMS) or Two-Stage PLS-SEM incorporating explicit quadratic terms ($PP^2$) to test the inverted-U personalization-reactance curve ($P_1$) alongside a multiplicative product indicator ($ESAT \times Arousal$) to validate the permission-kinetic energy interaction ($P_{5b}$), supplemented by Johnson-Neyman floodlight analysis to identify exact ego depletion thresholds ($P_{7a}, P_{7b}$). 2. Cross-Lagged Panel Modeling (Testing P8): To empirically capture the negative recursive feedback loop ($P_8$) across sequential shopping episodes without violating cross-sectional causality assumptions, researchers should implement a three-wave Random-Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (RI-CLPM) linking Time $t$ depletion-induced impulse purchases and post-purchase regret to Time $t+1$ cumulative e-satisfaction and leftward shifts in privacy tolerance thresholds. **Table 8: Conceptual Proposition Status and Recommended Empirical Testing Strategy** | Proposition | Hypothesized Mechanism / Path | Conceptual & Literature Status | Recommended Testing Strategy | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **P1** | Inverted-U Personalization $\rightarrow$ Measurable Surveillance Reactance | Under-tested in impulse buying (requires nonlinear validation) | Polynomial Regression / RSA ($PP^2$) + privacy/control moderators | | **P2 & P3** | Accuracy $\rightarrow$ Fluency/ESAT;
